event.title: Dedicated vector databases strengths
event.summary: Dedicated vector databases (Pinecone, Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus, Chroma) outperform pgvector through massive scale support (billions vs. millions of vectors), superior latency (4-8ms vs. struggle at scale), purpose-built hybrid search with efficient filtering, and managed operations eliminating DevOps overhead. They employ specialized indexing algorithms, distributed architecture, and query optimization unavailable to pgvector—justifying their adoption when vector search is central to the system.

event.title: pgvector capabilities and limits
event.summary: pgvector supports HNSW (graph-based, ~30× faster queries than IVFFlat, 95%+ recall out-of-box) and IVFFlat (memory-efficient, faster builds) indexes with a 2,000-dimension limit on standard vector type. It scales adequately to 5–10M vectors but experiences memory pressure and recall degradation beyond 10M; performance degrades sharply at 50M+ vectors without quantization. Known pain points include post-filter degradation, MVCC bloat from updates, memory eviction when working sets exceed RAM, and difficulty with metadata filtering without iterative scans (available in 0.8+).

findings.claim: pgvector enforces a hard dimension cap of 2,000 for HNSW and IVFFlat indexes on the standard vector type; halfvec extends this to 4,000 dimensions due to PostgreSQL's 8-kilobyte page size constraint.
findings.source_title: How to scale vector search in Postgres (pgvector) for RAG and AI agents
findings.quote: pgvector enforces a hard cap of 2,000 dimensions for HNSW and IVFFlat indexes. The halfvec type raises this to 4,000 dimensions.

findings.claim: HNSW achieves ~30× gains in QPS and p99 latency versus IVFFlat at 99% recall, with recent binary quantization versions delivering 100×+ build speedups; HNSW memory usage is 2–5× higher than IVFFlat.
findings.source_title: pgvector performance: Benchmark results and 5 ways to boost performance
findings.quote: HNSW plus binary quantization achieved approximately 100×+ build speedups with binary quantization and ~30× gains in QPS and p99 versus IVFFlat.

findings.claim: pgvector scales adequately to 5–10M vectors; at 10M documents with 1,536-dimensional embeddings on reasonably sized instances, HNSW returns top-10 results in under 10ms; performance becomes problematic beyond 50M vectors without quantization or partitioning.
findings.source_title: pgvector Explained: Complete Guide for Engineers Building RAG & AI Search
findings.quote: At 10M documents with 1,536-dimensional embeddings, an HNSW index returns top-10 results in under 10ms.

findings.claim: pgvector 0.8+ introduced iterative HNSW scans to improve filtering without sequential scan fallback; prior versions experienced severe post-filter degradation where metadata filters would eliminate most index candidates.
findings.source_title: How to scale vector search in Postgres (pgvector) for RAG and AI agents
findings.quote: pgvector 0.8+ addresses this with iterative index scans which keep pulling more candidates from the index until enough rows pass the WHERE clause.

findings.claim: HNSW indexes don't reclaim space from deleted rows, causing index bloat; MVCC bloat from updates accumulates dead tuples, shrinking the effective candidate pool and degrading recall in production.
findings.quote: HNSW indexes don't reclaim space from deleted rows, causing index bloat over time.

findings.claim: Switch to dedicated vector databases when processing 10M+ vectors, requiring sub-10ms p99 latency at scale, or facing high-churn multi-tenant workloads; standard pgvector scales best under ~10M vectors for active workloads.
findings.source_title: pgvector vs Vector Database: When to Use Each
findings.quote: Switch to dedicated databases when processing 10M+ vectors or requiring sub-10ms latency at scale.

event.report_md:
## TL;DR
- For "small" RAG (roughly under 5–10M vectors), pgvector is the default winner: sub-20ms queries at 1M vectors with >95% recall, no separate service to run [7][3].
- The tradeoff line isn't a single number — it's where **scale, latency SLAs, and ops tolerance** collectively outgrow Postgres, typically 10M+ vectors and hardening toward 50M+ [5][10].
- Cost strongly favors pgvector at small scale: ~$300–1,200/month vs Pinecone $2,500+, a 3–5x edge when you avoid a duplicate datastore [9].
- Filtered search (the production norm) actually favors pgvector; Pinecone runs ~37% slower at low concurrency in one comparison [9].
- Choose a dedicated DB when vector search is the core workload at 10M–100M+ scale, sub-10ms p99 at scale, or zero-DevOps managed operation is required [5][10][6].

## Where pgvector holds up
pgvector runs inside Postgres, eliminating a separate managed service, and handles ~2M vectors without special tuning [7]. It supports HNSW and IVFFlat indexes; HNSW delivers ~30x QPS and p99 gains over IVFFlat at 99% recall, plus ~150x faster builds in recent versions [2]. At 10M documents with 1,536-dim embeddings, HNSW returns top-10 results in under 10ms on reasonable instances [3]. It scales adequately to 5–10M vectors for active workloads [3][5]. A standard 2,000-dimension cap applies (4,000 with halfvec), which covers common embedding models [1]. For filtered retrieval — nearly all production RAG — pgvector often outperforms dedicated services on cost and latency [9]. With the pgvectorscale extension, one May 2025 benchmark showed 471 QPS at 99% recall on 50M vectors versus Qdrant's 41 QPS [8].

## Where dedicated vector DBs pull ahead
Beyond ~10M vectors pgvector hits memory pressure, recall degradation, HNSW index bloat from deletes, and MVCC bloat from updates; performance degrades sharply past 50M without quantization or partitioning [3][4][5]. Dedicated systems are purpose-built for this: Milvus handles hundreds of millions to billions of vectors via distributed architecture, unconstrained by Postgres's single-instance limits [6]. Qdrant and Weaviate lead filtered-search performance with complex filters, and Pinecone's serverless model removes capacity planning and DevOps entirely [6]. Reported latencies include Qdrant ~4ms p50 and Pinecone ~8ms p50 at scale [6]. Weaviate builds hybrid (semantic + keyword) search into its core natively [6].

## The tradeoff line
Expert consensus: start new production RAG on pgvector unless you have a strong reason otherwise, treating it as the default under roughly 100K–50M vectors [10]. Switch to a dedicated database when processing 10M+ vectors, needing sub-10ms p99 at scale, or running high-churn multi-tenant workloads [5]. For a genuinely small RAG system, cost and operational simplicity — not raw performance — are the decisive factors, and both point to pgvector [9][10].

## Open questions
- Benchmarks vary by hardware, index config, and dataset; the 50M-vector pgvectorscale vs Qdrant figures come from a single source and need independent replication [8].
- How hybrid/keyword search quality compares between pgvector (plus Postgres full-text) and native hybrid engines was not established in depth [6].
- Multi-tenant isolation and high-update-churn behavior for pgvector at mid-scale remains under-characterized beyond noted bloat issues [4][5].
